mgl-40a-s3-agriculture.summary: MGL c. 40A, § 3 says a zoning ordinance or bylaw may not prohibit, unreasonably regulate, or require a special permit for the use of land for the primary purpose of commercial agriculture, or for structures on that land used for that purpose. The same section says those activities may be limited to parcels of 5 acres or more, or to parcels of 2 acres or more if the sale of products from that use on the parcel generates at least $1,000 per acre a year based on gross sales dollars, in an area not zoned for agriculture. Land divided by a public or private way or a waterway is treated as one parcel. The section does not exempt land or structures from flood-plain or wetlands regulations. For this section, agriculture has the meaning in MGL c. 128, § 1A. Read § 1A before treating a particular animal operation as agriculture under § 3. This entry does not decide whether a parcel meets the acreage or sales test.
mgl-40a-s3-agriculture.confirm_role: The officer who enforces zoning where the land is. The statute is state law.

amherst-3-21-livestock.summary: Amherst General Bylaw § 3.21(C), Urban Livestock or Poultry, says raising or keeping livestock or poultry for private purposes is permitted and regulated under that bylaw, other local and Commonwealth regulations, and the zoning bylaw. Before acquiring the animals, the property owner registers with the Health Department. The Health Director reviews the application after consultation with the Animal Welfare Officer, and may approve it, deny it, or approve it with conditions. Registrants permit inspections, including inspections the Animal Welfare Officer may require under MGL c. 129, § 7. Notice goes to property owners within 300 feet. Where no zoning special permit is required, the Health Director waits more than 14 days after that mailing before acting, and holds an administrative hearing if the owners of a majority of the neighboring properties object. The Health Director may promulgate regulations after consulting the Animal Welfare Officer and the Agricultural Commission.
amherst-3-21-livestock.caveat: The enclosure, feed, waste, and odor standards in § 3.21(C)(1) are written for domesticated fowl and rabbits. Read that subsection before applying those numbers to cattle.
amherst-3-21-livestock.confirm_role: Amherst Health Department. The bylaw also names the Animal Welfare Officer.

amherst-3-47-rtf.summary: Amherst General Bylaw § 3.47, in the June 2026 general bylaws, recognizes a right to farm. The definition of farming includes raising livestock, including horses, and keeping and raising poultry, swine, cattle, sheep, cavies such as rabbits, ratites, camelids, and other domesticated animals for food or other purposes, including bees and fur-bearing animals. It also includes processing and packaging the farm's agricultural output and operating a farmer's market or farm stand. The bylaw says its protections are for operations conducted in accordance with generally accepted agricultural practices, and that it does not supersede local, Commonwealth, or federal laws or regulations or private covenants. It does not impose a land-use regulation, which the bylaw says is the subject of statute or the zoning bylaw. Complaints may be filed with the Town Manager, who forwards them to the Agricultural Commission.
amherst-3-47-rtf.confirm_role: Town of Amherst. The bylaw routes complaints through the Town Manager.

amherst-zoning-5-013.summary: Amherst Zoning Bylaw § 5.013, in the December 2025 zoning bylaw, treats raising or keeping livestock or poultry for use by residents of the premises as an accessory use in selected residential districts, and says it shall not be permitted in other districts. It is allowed by right in the Outlying Residence (R-O) and Low-Density Residence (R-LD) districts. In the General Residence (R-G), Village Center Residence (R-VC), and Neighborhood Residence (R-N) districts, only hens, ducks, pigeons, doves, and domesticated rabbits, including hares, may be kept as an accessory use. On those properties, roosters, geese, swans, turkeys, pheasants, peacocks, guinea fowl, pygmy goats, potbellied pigs, and any other livestock or poultry are not permitted unless the Zoning Board of Appeals grants a special permit. The cap in those districts is a combined total of 12 adult fowl and rabbits, counting only reproductively mature animals. Enclosures and shelters are set at least 10 feet from property lines and 20 feet from residential structures on adjacent property, with at least 10 square feet of open yard per adult animal. Registration with the Health Department is required in all cases. Section 5.0134 says no provision of § 5.013 applies to farm properties or agricultural operations recognized under MGL c. 40A, § 3.
amherst-zoning-5-013.confirm_role: Town of Amherst. Special permits under this section go to the Zoning Board of Appeals.

mgl-94-s120-license.summary: MGL c. 94, § 120 says no person shall engage in the slaughter of livestock or poultry without a license from the Department, and no person shall process or manufacture meat or poultry products in an establishment without a license from the Department. People in that business apply annually. Read 105 CMR 500.030(F) beside this statute: that subsection states a household-use exemption from 105 CMR 500.000. This entry does not decide which one applies to a particular slaughter.
mgl-94-s120-license.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Public Health. The board of health in the town may also have a role.

cmr-105-500-030-household.summary: 105 CMR 500.030(F) says the slaughter by a person of livestock or poultry of that person's own raising, on that person's own premises, and the preparation of the carcasses and food products on those premises exclusively for use by that person, members of the household, and nonpaying guests and employees, is exempt from regulation under 105 CMR 500.000. The animals have to be healthy, and the slaughter and processing have to be done under sanitary standards that produce food that is sound, clean, and fit for human food. The same regulation says authorized inspectors may inspect to confirm that an exempt operation meets those conditions. Compare the Department policy FP-03, which says product from a private-use slaughter may not be sold or given away.
cmr-105-500-030-household.caveat: The regulation includes use by nonpaying guests and employees. Policy FP-03 says the product may not be sold or given away. Read both before relying on either sentence.
cmr-105-500-030-household.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Public Health. The board of health in the town may also have a role.

dph-fp-03-sale-and-household.summary: Department of Public Health policy FP-03 says domesticated meat and poultry whose product is intended for sale as food must be slaughtered and processed in a USDA FSIS inspected facility, under mandatory or exempt USDA inspection, and that USDA-inspected facilities are subject to licensure by the Department. The policy lists rabbits among examples of game animals that may be inspected by USDA under a voluntary fee-for-inspection program. The same policy says a person who raises meat or poultry and slaughters and processes it for personal use does not first need a permit from the Department or the local board of health, and that the product may not be sold or given away and is only for the owner, immediate family, and nonpaying guests. This is a Department policy, not a statute.
dph-fp-03-sale-and-household.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Public Health. The board of health in the town may also have a role.

cmr-105-500-030-rabbits-and-license.summary: 105 CMR 500.030(A)(1) includes people who slaughter or process wild animals raised commercially for wholesale, and it names rabbits as an example. It says those animals are included in livestock or poultry, and their products in meat or poultry. Subsection (E) says no person shall slaughter or process livestock or poultry, or operate a slaughter or processing facility, without a valid license from the Department. An applicant has to document that the operation is currently inspected by USDA FSIS or is exempt from that inspection. No license is issued without that documentation. Read this with policy FP-03, which says meat intended for sale has to come from a USDA-inspected facility that is also licensed by the Department.
cmr-105-500-030-rabbits-and-license.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Public Health. The board of health in the town may also have a role.

dph-market-permit.summary: The Department of Public Health says a food vendor that operates in a temporary location, including a farmers market, must have a permit for certain activities. The local board of health requires a temporary food establishment permit and compliance with parts of the retail food code, 105 CMR 590. The same page says some activities of a non-permanent operation do not require a retail food permit. Read the current list on that page for the product being sold. Meat and poultry are not assumed to be on the no-permit list. Confirm with the board of health in the town where the market is held.
dph-market-permit.citation: DPH, food establishments at events and farmers markets
dph-market-permit.confirm_name: Board of health where the market is held
dph-market-permit.confirm_role: Local board of health. The Department of Public Health publishes the questions-and-answers page.

mdar-farmers-market-guide.summary: MDAR's guide says that under MGL c. 101, § 15, farmers may sell fruits, vegetables, or other farm products raised or produced by them or their family at farmers markets without a hawkers or peddlers license. The guide is agency guidance. Other rules still apply to the product. Run a separate lookup for eggs, meat, or poultry before treating a market sale as covered by this sentence alone.
mdar-farmers-market-guide.citation: MDAR, A guide to selling at farmers' markets

mgl-101-s15-farm-products.summary: MGL c. 101, § 15 says the hawkers and peddlers provisions of that chapter do not apply to a person who peddles only fish obtained by that person's own labor or the labor of the family, or fruits, vegetables, or other farm products raised or produced by that person or the family. The section also sets aside persons licensed under MGL c. 94, § 40 for the sale of eggs or milk products, except frozen desserts. MDAR's farmers-market guide cites this section for sales at a farmers market. The statute is about hawkers and peddlers. It does not say anything about inspection of meat, grading of eggs, or a local food permit.
mgl-101-s15-farm-products.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources, for the farmers-market reading of this section. A local board of health still permits food sales.

cfr-381-10-a3-household.summary: 9 CFR 381.10(a)(3) says the federal inspection requirements for processing poultry do not apply to a person who slaughters poultry of that person's own raising, and processes and transports the products, exclusively for use by that person, members of the household, and nonpaying guests and employees. The poultry has to be healthy and slaughtered and processed under sanitary standards that produce food that is sound, clean, and fit for human food. Shipping containers have to bear the producer's name and address and the statement Exempted—P.L. 90-492. This is a federal exemption. It does not speak to the Massachusetts household exemption in 105 CMR 500.030(F), which is a separate text.

cfr-381-10-c-1000.summary: 9 CFR 381.10(c) says the Poultry Products Inspection Act and the regulations do not apply to a poultry producer for poultry of that producer's own raising on that producer's own farm which the producer slaughters, if three conditions are met: the producer slaughters not more than 1,000 poultry during the calendar year for which the exemption is being determined; the producer does not buy or sell poultry products other than those produced from poultry raised on that farm; and none of the poultry moves in commerce as that word is defined in 9 CFR 381.1. Read the definition of commerce before treating this as an in-state rule. Massachusetts still has its own license and protocol requirements. See 105 CMR 500.031(J) and MGL c. 94, § 120.

cmr-105-500-031-poultry.summary: 105 CMR 500.031(J)(1) says all poultry producers and sellers shall comply with the federal exemptions at 9 CFR 381.10. Subsection (J)(3) says non-eviscerated poultry may not be sold, unless under a religious exemption in 105 CMR 500.030(H). Subsection (J)(10) says a person who slaughters or processes poultry for sale in a small on-farm operation under a USDA exemption shall comply with the Department's written protocols for that activity. Subsection (J)(9) says a person who slaughters or processes poultry for sale with a mobile poultry processing unit has to follow the Department's written protocols and has to be licensed. A federal exemption does not, by itself, remove the state license in MGL c. 94, § 120 and 105 CMR 500.030(E).
cmr-105-500-031-poultry.caveat: The Department's written protocols for small on-farm processing were not copied into this entry. Confirm with the Food Protection Program whether the current protocol limits the form of the bird, including any whole-bird condition, and whether sales have to stay in Massachusetts.
cmr-105-500-031-poultry.confirm_role: Massachusetts Department of Public Health. The board of health in the town may also have a role.

cmr-330-5-03-eggs.summary: 330 CMR 5.03 says all eggs for sale at retail in Massachusetts shall be grade AA, A, B, or not graded, and shall be in containers so marked or branded, with letters not less than three-eighths of an inch in height. Not graded means an egg that has not been candled to determine whether it meets AA, A, or B, and that is not inedible, a Loss, or a Leaker. An edible egg that does not conform to AA, A, or B may only be sold as a Check or Stain for further processing, or sold at the site of production directly from the producer to the household consumer. No person shall sell a Check, Stain, inedible egg, Loss, or Leaker as not graded. A retail sale marked not graded is not the same thing as a sale of eggs that failed AA, A, and B.

mdar-egg-handling.summary: MDAR's sheet for backyard egg producers says a producer may size and grade eggs or not, and must describe what is in the carton. It says many small producers identify eggs as Not Graded and Not Sized, also called nest run, meaning the eggs were not candled or weighed and were packed without sorting. It says all eggs, including those, should be clean and have no visible breakage. Grading questions go to the Division of Animal Health. This is an agency sheet. The grades themselves are in 330 CMR 5.03.
mdar-egg-handling.citation: MDAR, Safe egg handling for backyard egg producers

mdar-eggs-retail-permit.summary: A March 8, 2022 MDAR guidance document for farms says a retail food code permit is not required for farms selling whole, uncut fresh fruits and vegetables, unprocessed honey, pure maple products, or farm fresh eggs which are stored and maintained at 45°F (7.2°C) or less. This is guidance about the retail food code. It is not a grading rule. Read it beside 330 CMR 5.03 and confirm the current permit practice with the board of health for the town where the eggs are sold.
mdar-eggs-retail-permit.confirm_name: Board of health where the eggs are sold
mdar-eggs-retail-permit.confirm_role: Local board of health. MDAR's Division of Animal Health answers grading questions.

cfr-303-1-cattle-custom.summary: 9 CFR 303.1(a)(1) says federal inspection of the preparation of products does not apply to a person who slaughters livestock of that person's own raising, and prepares the meat, exclusively for use by that person, the household, and nonpaying guests and employees. Subsection (a)(2) says the same about custom slaughter of cattle, sheep, swine, or goats delivered by the owner, and about custom preparation of those animals, when the products are exclusively for use in that owner's household by the owner, household members, nonpaying guests, and employees. The custom operator has to meet the conditions in that paragraph, including keeping any products prepared for sale separate from the custom products and plainly marking the custom products Not for Sale immediately after preparation, until they are delivered to the owner. A sale of the live animal is a different transaction from a sale of meat. If a buyer becomes the owner and then delivers the animal for custom slaughter, the conditions in (a)(2) are the ones to read. This entry does not decide whether a particular sale meets them.

cfr-303-1-cattle-not-for-sale.summary: 9 CFR 303.1(a)(2) marks custom-prepared cattle products Not for Sale and limits them to use in the owner's household. Selling the meat is outside that exemption. Meat from cattle that is for sale has to be read against the inspection requirement those exemptions are carved out of, and against the Massachusetts license in MGL c. 94, § 120 and 105 CMR 500.030. Confirm the inspection status of the plant with USDA FSIS and the Food Protection Program.

chicopee-zoning-farms.summary: Chicopee Zoning Ordinance Chapter 275, Article IV, lists farms, nurseries, and truck gardens as permitted uses in Residential A districts and in Residential B districts. The pages checked on October 14, 2026 did not show that phrase as a permitted use in every other district. The ordinance does not, in the text checked, define farm or name rabbits, poultry, or cattle. State law MGL c. 40A, § 3 is a separate limit on how zoning may treat commercial agriculture. Confirm the district of the parcel on the zoning map with the building department.
chicopee-zoning-farms.citation: Chicopee Zoning Ordinance ch. 275, art. IV
chicopee-zoning-farms.confirm_role: City of Chicopee, for the zoning district of a parcel

chicopee-ch-144-fowl.summary: Chicopee Chapter 144 says: "No fowl shall be kept or maintained within the limits of the City except where allowed by rules and regulations promulgated by the Board of Health." The Board of Health rule text was not in the ordinance page checked on October 14, 2026. The ordinance also says no swine shall be kept except for immediate slaughter; swine are outside the species in this lookup. This entry does not restate a Board of Health species limit, setback, or permit fee, because that text was not in the source checked.
chicopee-ch-144-fowl.caveat: The Board of Health rules that this sentence points to are not on file here.
chicopee-ch-144-fowl.confirm_role: City of Chicopee. Ask for the current fowl rules before keeping poultry.

chicopee-ch-144-cattle.summary: Chicopee Chapter 144 says no person shall permit any sheep, goat, swine, mule, ass, horse, or meat cattle belonging to that person, or under that person's control, to go at large or depasture in any street, lane, alley, or on any common in the city. It also says no person shall permit a goat, sheep, swine, horse, mule, ox, or cow to go upon a sidewalk except to cross to or from an adjoining enclosure, and no person shall permit a horse, cow, swine, goat, or other grazing animal to go at large in any street.
chicopee-ch-144-cattle.confirm_role: City of Chicopee. The chapter also names animal control officers and the police.

hadley-rtf.summary: A copy of a Hadley Right to Farm bylaw hosted by the Massachusetts Association of Agricultural Commissions says its purpose is to explain the right to farm under Article 97 and state law, including MGL c. 40A, § 3, c. 90, § 9, c. 111, § 125A, and c. 128, § 1A. It says the bylaw applies to jurisdictional areas within the town. It defines a farm as any parcel or contiguous parcels of land, or water bodies, used for the primary purpose of commercial agriculture, or accessory to that purpose. It says a person with a complaint about a farm may file a grievance with the Select Board, the Zoning Enforcement Officer, or the Board of Health, and that filing the grievance does not suspend other remedies.
hadley-rtf.caveat: Unverified. This summary was taken from a community copy, not from a posting on the Town of Hadley's own site, and the full bylaw was not re-read as adopted text. Do not rely on it until you read the town's copy and confirm it with the Town Clerk.
hadley-rtf.confirm_role: The community copy also names the Zoning Enforcement Officer and the Board of Health for grievances.

leverett-ch-20-rtf.summary: Leverett Chapter 20, in the 2025 town code, recognizes a right to farm. The farming definition includes raising of livestock and keeping and raising poultry, swine, cattle, sheep, goats, ratites, camelids, and other domesticated animals for food and other agricultural purposes, including bees. Rabbits are not named. Section 20-5 says the bylaw does not supersede or add regulations different from state or federal land-use rules, or from other town bylaws, including the zoning bylaws and Board of Health regulations. The 2025 code states that Board of Health regulations are not included in the code.
leverett-ch-20-rtf.caveat: No Board of Health animal regulation from Leverett is on file. Ask the Board before assuming none exists.
leverett-ch-20-rtf.confirm_role: Town of Leverett. Grievances in the bylaw also go to the Select Board, the zoning enforcement officer, or the Board of Health.

leverett-zoning-2242.summary: Leverett Zoning Bylaw § 2242 says horses and other animals, including pigs, chickens, and other farm animals, used for non-commercial or non-agricultural purposes, may be stabled as an accessory use within the RR and RV districts. It names pigs and chickens. It does not name rabbits, turkeys, or cattle. Whether an animal is a farm animal under that sentence, and whether a use is non-commercial, is a question for the zoning enforcement officer. Commercial agriculture that meets MGL c. 40A, § 3 is addressed in a different row of the use table.

leverett-zoning-40a.summary: The Leverett zoning use table, in the bylaw that includes the 2020 changes, lists agriculture, silviculture, horticulture, floriculture, or viticulture exempt from zoning regulations pursuant to MGL c. 40A, § 3 as a yes use across the districts in that row. The bylaw does not itself decide whether a parcel meets the acreage or sales test in § 3. Read MGL c. 40A, § 3 for that test. A 2026 draft of zoning changes was not adopted text and is not summarized here.

south-hadley-rtf.summary: The South Hadley Right to Farm bylaw says its purpose is to restate the right to farm under Article 97 and state law, including MGL c. 40A, § 3, c. 90, § 9, c. 111, § 125A, and c. 128, § 1A. Its definition of farming includes breeding of livestock, including horses, and keeping and raising poultry, swine, cattle, sheep, goats, rabbits, ratites, camelids, and other domesticated animals for food and other agricultural purposes, including bees and furbearing animals such as mink. It says the benefits and protections apply exclusively to commercial agricultural operations conducted in accordance with generally accepted agricultural practices and local zoning and other regulations.
south-hadley-rtf.citation: South Hadley Right to Farm bylaw
south-hadley-rtf.confirm_role: For the adopted text. Zoning questions go to the zoning enforcement officer. Health questions go to the Board of Health.

south-hadley-boh-permit.summary: The South Hadley Board of Health livestock regulations say no person, firm, or corporation shall keep, in any building or on any premises in the town, any horses, cows, ducks, geese, goats, guinea pigs, chickens, pigeons, rabbits, sheep, or any other fowl or animals without a Stable and Livestock Permit from the Board of Health. Permits expire annually on March 31 and may be revoked for cause. Dogs and cats are excluded only from section 1. The page cites the town bylaws, Chapter 12, Section 3, and MGL c. 111, § 155, as authority. Later sections on the same page address cleanliness, manure, carcass disposal within 24 hours, immunization records required by the Division of Animal Health, and a court fine of not more than $100.
south-hadley-boh-permit.citation: South Hadley Board of Health livestock regulations, § 1
south-hadley-boh-permit.confirm_name: Sharon D. Hart, Public Health Director
south-hadley-boh-permit.confirm_role: South Hadley Public Health Department, 116 Main Street, Room M2

southwick-ch-140-rtf.summary: Southwick Chapter 140 says its purpose is to state the right to farm under Article 97 and state statutes, including MGL c. 40A, § 3. It recognizes a right to farm in the town. The bylaw's description of farming includes keeping and raising poultry, swine, sheep, cattle, ratites, and camelids, and other domesticated animals for food and other agricultural purposes, including bees and fur-bearing animals. It says the described activities may occur on holidays, weekdays, and weekends, by night or day, and include incidental noise, odors, dust, and fumes associated with normally accepted agricultural practices. The benefits and protections are for commercial agricultural operations conducted in accordance with generally accepted agricultural practices. The bylaw does not name rabbits.
southwick-ch-140-rtf.caveat: Rabbits are not named. The catch-all is other domesticated animals kept for food.
southwick-ch-140-rtf.confirm_role: Town of Southwick. The bylaw also points back to state statutes enforced by other officers.

southwick-ch-69-at-large.summary: Southwick § 69-12.1 makes it the duty of the Animal Control Officer, and any assistant appointed by the Select Board, to apprehend any livestock or farm animal found running at large and to tell the owner to recapture and contain the animals. The officer keeps a record of the incident and notifies the owner, or posts notice with the Police Department if the owner is unknown. The bylaw's schedule for a violation is a written warning for a first offense and $10 for a second and each subsequent offense. In § 69-2, farm animal includes poultry and species of cattle raised for commercial or subsistence purposes. Domestic rabbits are not in that definition.
southwick-ch-69-at-large.confirm_role: Town of Southwick, appointed by the Select Board
